rewrites.name: Misiones
rewrites.summary:
No Misiones-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors; provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real — the silence reflects documentation, not demonstrated safety.

What a visitor faces is the national risk picture: a March 2026 report recorded at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year and the highest of the observatory's ten recorded years — one every 38 hours — predominantly by security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, with beatings the main modality. On documents: the 2012 Gender Identity Law (legal gender change without medical intervention, an 'X' document marker since 2021) remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed, so a visitor cannot count on the formal protections being honoured.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context is national policy turbulence: the national government eliminated the ministry for women, gender and diversity and dismissed trans hires made under the trans employment-quota law (1% of public-sector posts), which activists say is no longer being implemented; a February 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments. The hate-crime surge is attributed to the government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people, and attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of an LGBTIQ+ organisation president in another province; activists describe the resulting situation as 'chaotic, desperate'.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data from the national monitoring: of the 227 recorded hate crimes in 2025, 62.5% of victims (142 of 227) were trans women or travestis, and 64.8% of cases (147) were physical violence against bodily integrity; the quota-law dismissals fall mainly on trans residents employed in the public sector.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: An April 2025 Washington Blade feature describing the 'chaotic, desperate' situation is no longer retrievable, so its account cannot be re-verified. No province-specific enforcement or incident data exists to confirm or exclude local risk; beyond activists' report that the 'X' document marker is no longer guaranteed, current screening practice is undocumented.

rewrites.name: Neuquén
rewrites.summary:
No Neuquén-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented; the province is listed among the units classified "no sub-national signal", with the explicit caveat that most such provinces retain contravención/faltas (police infraction) powers — the instrument an NGO survey holds responsible for most arrests of trans and travesti people — so "no signal" here means "no documentation", not "no exposure".

For a visitor, exposure in practice runs through the same instruments: the February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply here as to all provinces, within a deteriorating national picture (a record 227 anti-LGBT hate crimes in 2025, up 62%).

Residents also stand under the contravención/faltas (police infraction) powers that the NGO survey identifies as the instrument behind most arrests of trans and travesti people.

rewrites.name: Río Negro
rewrites.summary:
The provincial statute reserving at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people — one of only a handful of provinces with such a law — signals a provincial official posture better than the national baseline, though the surveys reviewed found none of these quota laws actually being complied with.

For a visitor the operative exposure is the national one: the contravención/faltas (police infraction) powers remain, and the February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply here too. Because national trans-death counts are small enough that one provincial case is a real signal, the 2024 national MuMaLa registry entry attributing a travesti victim to this province (jointly with a neighbouring province) counts as a local risk signal.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context is national policy turbulence: the national government eliminated the ministry for women, gender and diversity and dismissed trans hires made under the trans employment-quota law (1% of public-sector posts), which activists say is no longer being implemented; a February 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments. The hate-crime surge is attributed to the government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people, and attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of an LGBTIQ+ organisation president in another province; activists describe the resulting situation as 'chaotic, desperate'.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 1% travesti/trans employment statute is a resident-only mechanism a visitor never uses; its visitor-facing value is the official-posture signal it carries (non-compliant as of the surveys reviewed).

Resident-facing data from the national monitoring: of the 227 recorded hate crimes in 2025, 62.5% of victims (142 of 227) were trans women or travestis, and 64.8% of cases (147) were physical violence against bodily integrity; the quota-law dismissals fall mainly on trans residents employed in the public sector.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Compliance with the provincial quota statute is documented only as of the surveys reviewed (non-compliant); whether it is enforced today is not documented. The 2024 registry entry attributing a victim to this province jointly with a neighbouring province is not further detailed in the sources reviewed.

rewrites.name: San Juan
rewrites.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.

For a visitor the operating position is the national one: the 2012 Gender Identity Law (legal gender change without medical intervention, an 'X' document marker since 2021) remains formally in force but activists report it is no longer guaranteed, and a February 2025 executive decree bars under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, applying to every province.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation flux, not local risk: legal experts and LGBTI+ organisations call the February 2025 decrees unconstitutional and say abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth; the decrees face judicial challenge. The broader national turbulence includes the elimination of the ministry for women, gender and diversity, the end of implementation of the trans employment-quota law (1% of public-sector posts), and activists' description of a 'chaotic, desperate' situation.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing national mechanisms are the changed prison placement rules for trans detainees and the trans employment-quota law, whose dismissals fell on trans public-sector staff; no division-specific resident data is documented in the sources reviewed.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the amended national regime survives the judicial challenge is unresolved at this writing. No division-specific enforcement or incident record is separately documented, so the assessment rests on the national dossier.

Community representatives say the community faces a 'chaotic, desperate' situation; the 2012 gender identity law (legal gender change without medical intervention, an 'X' document marker since 2021) remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed.

National-framework reporting (6 February 2025): the government published two decrees — one amending the gender identity law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, and one altering prison-sentencing rules to change the placement of trans detainees; legal experts and LGBTI+ organisations call both decrees unconstitutional and say abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and the decrees face judicial challenge. They apply nationally, to every state/province.

rewrites.name: Santa Fe
rewrites.summary:
No Santa Fe-specific statute or enforcement series with a source was found; the province is nonetheless one of the few that measures its own exposure — the provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that include transfemicidios and travesticidios (anti-trans killings), and national registers name provincial transfemicide victims — so local signals are better documented than in most provinces.

For a visitor the practical picture is the national one: at least 227 hate crimes on SOGI grounds in 2025 (+62% year-on-year, one every 38 hours, security-force-perpetrator cases doubled from 17 to 64), the February 2025 executive decrees amending the Gender Identity Law and prison housing apply to every province, and trans activists' testimony on a resulting hostile climate.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation flux, not local risk: legal experts and LGBTI+ organisations call the February 2025 decrees unconstitutional and say abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth; the decrees face judicial challenge. The broader national turbulence includes the elimination of the ministry for women, gender and diversity and the end of implementation of the trans employment-quota law (1% of public-sector posts); activists describe the resulting situation as 'chaotic, desperate'.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing measurement tools are the provincial violent-death statistics (including transfemicidios and travesticidios, i.e. anti-trans killings), the local observatory monitoring gender violence, and the national registers naming provincial transfemicide victims; these mechanisms themselves are never used by a visitor.
